name: Jamal Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a paramedic science course, so it's anatomy, first aid practicals with dummies and a lot of learning drug doses off by heart. I get up at four on Tuesdays and Thursdays to help my dad at our family bakery before lectures, and on Saturdays I drive the delivery van to cafés. I live with my parents and my grandad above the bakery on Fenn Street. We go to church on Sundays, and then Mum makes lunch for about ten people. It's a full week, but I like knowing where everyone is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought, and I'd say good. People have been told for years that machines will take everything, and mostly it's a lot of talk. At the bakery I'd say we've always had ovens that do the work, but you still need a baker to know when the bread's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved but I'd still worry about money. The course fees are on a loan, and I earn what the bakery pays me, which is not much. Paramedic jobs are steady, but the training is long, and there are few ambulance posts near us. So it's about money and places, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep the bakery mornings and the van on Saturdays, study at the kitchen table and put my placement hours first. I'd ask the ambulance trust about their student bursary. I wouldn't touch anything like AI. I know my drug doses, and I'd rather get them from my head than from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Nothing to be afraid of, though the loan sits in the back of my mind like a stone in a shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the bakery didn't have enough work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for a job in a care home or as a porter. My uncle Rui works in a hospital and he says there's always a porter job going. It's not glamorous, but it'd keep me in the hospital world and I'd learn how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather learn drug doses from your head. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because on a call there's no time to look at a screen. My tutor says the best paramedics have the numbers in their heads. If I rely on a device and it fails, a person could die. That's why I'm slow to trust new things.

say: People have been told for years that machines will take **everything**, and mostly it's talk.
You still need a baker to know when the bread is right.
think: I'd be relieved but still worry about **money**, because the loan is long and ambulance posts near us are few.
It's about money and places, not computers.
do: Keep the **bakery** mornings and the Saturday van, and put placement hours first.
Ask the ambulance trust about their student bursary.
Learn my drug doses from memory, not a screen.
feel: **Settled**, though the loan sits at the back of my mind like a stone in a shoe.
S0.quote: On a call there's no time to look at a screen.
fieldNote: Jamal's worries are the **loan** and the few local ambulance posts, not technology.
His reasons for avoiding AI are practical: no time on a call to look at a screen.

steps.text: Keep the early bakery shifts and the Saturday van round
Ask the ambulance trust about the student bursary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some jobs will change, and the people behind a desk will feel it before people with their hands. At the bakery I'd say don't believe the salesmen who say a machine can run the shop alone. At church I'd say look after each other if somebody loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my own job is fairly safe. Paramedics go to the person, carry them, calm the family. A computer can't do that, and the ambulance won't drive itself into a flat on the fifth floor. But the dispatch and the paperwork might go to software, and that changes how many people are needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the course. I'd get as much practice as I could on placement. I'd keep helping at the bakery, and I'd ask my dad whether we should think about delivering orders online, since the cafés are changing how they buy. I'd learn the dispatch system if the trust uses it, but only when I'm asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. I'm not scared for me, but I'm thinking of my cousins who work in offices, and of the bakery customers who might lose jobs and stop buying bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family would be most affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ines, who does customer service for an insurance company. Her bosses already said the chat bot is answering half the calls. She's twenty-five, with a baby, and her husband's work is up and down. We'd all help her, but it's a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family usually handle trouble like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We pull together. My grandad says you don't go to the state first, you go to family, then the church, then the state. I think that's right, and it's how we've always done it. But I know not everyone has that.

say: The people behind a **desk** will feel it before people with their hands.
At church I'd say we must look after each other if somebody loses work.
think: My job is fairly safe, because **paramedics** go to the person and carry them.
Dispatch and paperwork might move to software and change staffing.
do: Keep my head down, do the course and get as much **placement** practice as I can.
Ask my dad about taking online orders for the cafés.
Learn the dispatch system only when the trust asks.
feel: A little **uneasy**, mostly for my cousins in offices and for customers who might lose work.
S1.quote: My grandad says you don't go to the state first, you go to family, then the church, then the state.
fieldNote: Jamal feels safe in his own work but anxious about his **cousin** in customer service, whose firm already uses a chat bot.
His default answer to trouble is family first, then church, then the state.

steps.text: Do the course and log as many placement hours as possible
Ask my dad about taking online orders from the cafés
Help my cousin find work if her firm cuts hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a terrible thing to rush. Two years isn't time for anyone to sort out their lives. At church the priest would want to talk about it, and I'd say we should all pray and also do something sensible. At the bakery my dad would stay quiet and I'd know he's worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be frightened. I'd not be qualified for another two and a half years. The family has only the bakery and one part-time wage from Mum, and if the cafés stop ordering because their customers have no jobs, we'd be in trouble. I'd not know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the course going, because paramedics are hands-on and the last to be replaced. I'd work more at the bakery and ask the family to put some money by. I'd talk to our priest and the trust about any help. And I'd vote for anybody who promised to protect ordinary jobs, because I'd not trust the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd not be able to eat properly. It'd feel like the whole street was in trouble at once, and I'd not know who to turn to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should keep the bakery open as long as we can, and I'd work every morning. He'd say don't worry, but his hands would be shaking a little on the cup. I'd want to say sorry for not being able to help more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about the two years only?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's too fast for the old ways to catch up. The politicians would argue and nothing would happen. I'd rather something was done to slow it, like a law that says a person must be there for jobs like mine, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

say: It's a terrible thing to **rush**, because two years isn't time for anyone to sort out their lives.
We should pray and also do something sensible.
think: I'd be **frightened**: the family has only the bakery and one part-time wage.
If the cafés stop ordering, we're in trouble.
do: Keep the course going, because paramedics are hands-on and last to be **replaced**.
Work more at the bakery and ask the family to put money by.
Vote for anyone who promises to protect ordinary jobs.
feel: **Alarmed** and unable to eat properly, as if the whole street is in trouble at once.
S2.quote: I'd rather something was done to slow it, like a law that says a person must be there for jobs like mine
fieldNote: Jamal's fear is for the **bakery** and his dad, and he is not sure who to turn to.
He doubts politicians will act in two years but would still vote for protection of ordinary jobs.

steps.text: Work every bakery morning and keep the course going
Ask the family to put a little money by each week
Vote for whoever promises to protect ordinary jobs
Talk to our priest and the ambulance trust about help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, and a sensible person would use it. I'd tell my friends to learn a trade with their hands, or get a job in a hospital or care. At church I'd say we need to look after families, and that the bakery should think ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd still feel worried, but I'd feel there's time. I'd qualify in about three and a half years, and I'd have a year or two as a paramedic before the robots reach the road. It's a good job, and families will always want a person in their kitchen at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, take the first paramedic job near home, and keep helping my dad. I'd get a little money aside, around thirty pounds a month. I'd ask my dad to start taking orders from small businesses online, so the bakery isn't relying on cafés. I'd stay away from AI unless the trust trains us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to cope. I'd feel like I know what to do next, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the bakery to look like in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit smaller and surer. We'd maybe cut one delivery run, sell more to people in the street, and have a little website. My dad doesn't like screens, but I'd show him how. We'd keep the old recipes, because that's what people come for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if the ambulance jobs are fewer than you hoped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a private ambulance firm or as an emergency care assistant. It pays less, but it's still the work. I'd rather do a smaller version of the job I want than start something different.

say: Five years is something, and a sensible person would **use** it.
Learn a trade with your hands, or get a job in a hospital or care.
think: I'd still be worried, but there's time to qualify and work a year or two as a **paramedic**.
Families will always want a person in their kitchen at three in the morning.
do: Finish the course, take the first paramedic job near **home** and keep helping my dad.
Put thirty pounds a month aside.
Ask my dad to take online orders from small businesses.
feel: Anxious but able to **cope**, because I know what to do next.
S3.quote: I'd rather do a smaller version of the job I want than start something different.
fieldNote: More time lets Jamal plan for both his **career** and the bakery: a smaller, surer shop and a basic website.
He would rather do a smaller version of the job he wants than start something different.

steps.text: Finish the course and take the first paramedic job near home
Put thirty pounds a month aside
Help my dad build a small website for street customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and not to lose sleep over it. People have always had to adapt, and my grandad's generation saw big changes too. I'd tell everyone to do their job well and look after their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about my job. I'd be a paramedic for years before the robots arrive in about thirty. But I'd worry about the country, because ten years goes quickly, and the politicians would not prepare. I'd want to be settled by then, with a house and maybe a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, work as a paramedic and save for a place. I'd marry, if I met the right person, and I'd help my parents. I'd learn what the new technology does only when the job requires it. I'd keep a bit of savings, because you never know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, mostly. A little nervous, like before an exam, but I could sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd want to have sorted in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery's future. If my dad retires, I'd want someone to take it on, perhaps my younger brother, Tomas. I'd want it to be a place that still works if machines take over a lot of the jobs around us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your attitude to new technology over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit. If the ambulance trust makes me use something, I will. But I'd still check it against what I know. I think that's wise, not stubborn. My cousin says it's stubborn.

say: Ten years is a long time, so don't lose **sleep**, because people have always had to adapt.
Do your job well and look after your family.
think: I'd feel okay about my job, but worry that **politicians** won't prepare.
I'd want to be settled by then, with a house and maybe a family.
do: Finish the course, work as a paramedic and save for a **place**.
Help my parents and keep a bit of savings.
Learn new technology only when the job requires it.
feel: Content, mostly, and a little **nervous**, like before an exam.
S4.quote: I'd still check it against what I know. I think that's wise, not stubborn.
fieldNote: Jamal's long view is about **settling**: a house, family and the bakery's future with his brother Tomas.
He softens slightly on technology, but would still check it against what he knows.

steps.text: Work as a paramedic and save for a place of my own
Help my parents and plan the bakery's future with my brother
Keep to the ambulance trust's job and use new tools only when told

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one where nobody has time to get ready, and families like mine would be hit first. What would help is the government protecting hands-on jobs, my college giving us honest news, and families and the church holding together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me, who like the old ways, are not against progress. We just want it to be shown to work first. We're not afraid of work, but we are afraid of being left to sort it out alone.

headlineQuote: We're not afraid of work, but we are afraid of being left to sort it out alone.
portrait: Jamal is a 19-year-old **paramedic** student who helps at his family's bakery and lives above it with his parents and grandad.
He is traditional and resistant: he trusts family, church and his own memory over screens and AI.
He sees his own hands-on job as fairly safe, but fears for his cousin in customer service and for the bakery.
His plans are small and steady: finish the course, save a little, keep the family business going.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because nobody would have time to get ready and families like his would be hit first.
whatWouldHelp: The government protecting **hands-on** jobs, honest news from his college, and families and church holding together.
